text: Dr. Russell Meeuf CRN: 71294 & 79215 F 9:30-10:20 F 10:30-11:20 AD 326 & AD 227 ADMIN 346 rmeeuf@uidaho.edu JAMM 122: Multimedia Storytelling Course Description: This course introduces the basic principles of photographic and audio-video storytelling. Students will demonstrate competency through a series of hands-on assignments and through revision of their work. Learning Outcomes: Understand basic concepts in visual communication. Shoot photos and videos that communicate specific ideas or emotions. Learn to record and edit audio. Apply basic concepts of video editing. Understand how to work with photo, audio and video files, including how to share work online. Think about how issues of cultural diversity impact the process of visual communication. Book (OPTIONAL): Mark Blaine, The Digital Reporter’s Notebook (Routledge, 2014). Equipment: All student work will be completed on a smart phone. If students do not have access to a smart phone, instructions will be provided for renting digital cameras or audio recorders from media services. We will be practicing basic concepts for media communication, not advanced tutorials on professional equipment. You will develop your skills with more advanced equipment in other classes, depending on your individual major. That said, be sure that you familiarize yourself on the functioning of whatever equipment you choose to use. (If students have access to their own cameras (DSLRs for example), they are free to use them). Students should also have access to (1) a small camera grip and/or tripod, (2) a clip for attaching their smart phone to the grip or tripod, and (3) a microphone. See the software & equipment handout for recommendations. Software: Students will need access to a basic photo editor, audio editing software, and video editing software. I recommend that students purchase an Adobe Creative Cloud account in order to have access to professional level software in these different areas, but other options are acceptable for the class. See the software & equipment handout for more details. Course Policies: Each student will post their work on streaming sites such as SoundCloud, YouTube, or Vimeo. Make sure that you have an account and know how to use it. No late work will be accepted, especially as a result of technological setbacks. Part of the work of the class is to familiarize yourself with the basic processes of collecting, storing, editing, and sharing media files. Learning to complete this process under deadline is central to the learning outcomes of the class. Plan ahead! Your work in this class will require you to save and organize a variety of media files. For suggestions on efficient file storage, naming, and organization, see The Digital Reporter’s Notebook, chapters 37-39. Email is the best way to contact me outside of class, but please be courteous and respectful in the tone and wording of your emails to me. Also, please allow an appropriate amount of time for me to read and respond to your emails. I will not, however, accept work turned in by e-mail. I will also use email as my primary means of communication with the class, so please be sure that your email address is updated in the University's system and that you check your email regularly. Academic honesty is expected. Fabricating information and plagiarism are not tolerated. Any attempt to pass off written language or media content produced by someone else as your own will result in failure in the course. No exceptions. In order to learn, we must be open to the views of people different than ourselves. Please respect the uniqueness of your classmates and the opportunity we have to learn from one another. My goals for this course are that (1) all students, regardless of their backgrounds or individual perspectives, be well-served by this course, (2) that students' learning needs be addressed both in and out of class, and (3) that the diversity students bring to this class be viewed as a resource, strength and benefit. Please let me know if you have ideas about how to improve the effectiveness of the course for you personally or for other students or student groups. Reasonable accommodations are available for students who have documented temporary or permanent disabilities.  All accommodations must be approved through Disability Support Services located in the Idaho Commons Building, Room 306. Please meet with Gloria or Angela at the beginning of each semester to set up accommodations for the semester so that you may notify your instructor(s) early in the semester: 208-885-6307 or dss@uidaho.edu. Students should present a completed and signed Accommodation Checklist for the current semester from DSS when requesting accommodations.  If you do not have a current checklist both completed and signed, please visit the Disability Support Services office (Idaho Commons, Room 306) to obtain one. For more information, see:  http://www.uidaho.edu/studentaffairs/asap/dss If you have circumstances that may require different accommodations than outlined in the course policies, please consult with me as soon as possible. Assessment & Grading Multimedia Projects (100%): You will complete seven projects this term (five original projects and two revised and edited versions of a prior project). Each original project is worth 16% of your final grade, and the revised versions are each worth 10%. For each original project, if your first attempt fails to meet a set of basic criteria, you will be required to do it over. Violating any of the following guidelines on your work will result in an automatic do-over (or a zero on the assignment if it is your second attempt): Do NOT use images or audio that you do not have permission to use in your work. If you want to use music, make sure you use royalty free or public domain music. Do NOT shoot video in the vertical (portrait) mode. Shoot all video in the horizontal (landscape) mode. Course Outline: Topic: Out of Class: Assignment Due: In Class: Week 1 (1/13) Introduction Familiarize Yourself with Equipment and Software Introductions Week 2 (1/20) Audio Audio Storytelling Module Audio Stories Examples and Suggestions Week 3 (1/27) Audio Work on “This Idaho Life” This Idaho Life Week 4 (2/2) Audio-Photo Work on “This Idaho Life” (If needed) Basics of Photography Module This Idaho Life (Do-Over) Photo Examples and Suggestions Week 5 (2/10) Photo Work on “Street Photography” Street Photography Week 6 (2/17) Photo-Video Work on “Street Photography” (If needed) Basics of Video Module Street Photography (Do-Over) Montage Examples and Suggestions Week 7 (2/24) Video 1 Work on “Montage Video” Montage Video Week 8 (3/3) Video 1-Video 2 Work on “Montage Video” (if needed) Video Interviews Module Montage Video (Do-Over) Interview Examples and Suggestions Week 9 (3/10) Video 2 Work on “Video Interview” *****SPRING RECESS***** Week 10 (3/24) Video 2 Work on “Video Interview” Video Interview Week 11 (3/31) Video 2 Work on “Video Interview” (Do-Over or Edit) Video Interview (Do-Over or Edit) Week 12 (4/7) Video 2- Video 3 Work on “Video Interview” (Edit) Shooting Action Video Module Video Interview (Edit) Process Video Examples and Suggestions Week 13 (4/14) Video 3 Work on “Process Video” Week 14 (4/21) Video 3 Work on “Process Video” Process Video Week 15 (4/28) Video 3 Work on “Process Video” (Do-Over or Edit) Process Video (Do-Over or Edit) Week 16 (5/5) Video 3 Work on “Process Video” (Edit) Process Video (Edit) Assignment Descriptions: This Idaho Life: Find a friend or acquaintance who has a compelling story. The story can be funny, sad, thought-provoking, or mysterious, as long as it captures audience attention. It also has to be a story that your friend experienced personally (no “My dad knew a guy whose wife went skiing with Lindsey Lohan once”). Next, record your friend telling their story. Be sure to ask follow up questions and gather any other pertinent backstory. Then, using an audio editing program, produce a short audio segment about the friend and their story. This should not simply be a recording of them telling the story—your job is to tell the story using a mixture of your words and their words. Use your own narration to introduce the story and its teller. Explain why the story is significant or worth sharing with others. And then edit the story itself—are there moments when you can summarize the events in order to move through the narrative more swiftly? Is there important backstory that you should provide, either before the story or in the middle of it? What is the best way to share the story with a broad audience? Will you include music and when? The finished product should be 1:30 long. Post the story on SoundCloud and then link to it on the assignment link in bblearn. Tips: Remember that this is YOUR audio story, in which you share the story of your interview subject. I should hear your voice a lot as you set up and help tell the narrative, using select quotations from your interview. Street Photography: Find a public place and ask random people (i.e. people you do not know) if you can take their picture. Choose subjects who you think will make for a distinct or compelling visual image. The portraits can be of single individuals or of small groups. When you take the portrait, consider camera distance: closer portraits reveal more facial characteristics, but longer shots offer a stronger sense of their dress, body language, and the backdrop of the portrait. Also, consider the space around the subjects and the angle that you shoot them from—can you take advantage of an interesting backdrop? Feel free to be creative. Take 5 portraits, and for each subject have them sign a photo release form (available on Bblearn). Of the 5, only 2 can be in portrait mode. Post the pictures on the assignment link on bblearn. Tips: I’ll be grading you on your ability to experiment with camera distance and perspective, so make sure that there is some variety in your approaches to the different subjects. I’ll also be assessing your ability to use the rule of thirds, so make sure at least three of the shots are in “landscape” mode and employ the rule of thirds. You will probably need to take way more than 5 pictures. Take a bunch and choose your favorite five. Video Montage: Create a 30 second video montage that expresses a particular theme or idea (I will assign you a theme). The montage is a string of non-narrative images whose combination evokes a set of ideas or emotions. Remember to consider rhythm and pacing in your editing as you construct your montage. Additionally, be sure to use a variety of camera distances and camera angles as you shoot your subject matter. Post the video on Vimeo or YouTube and then link to it on the assignment link in bblearn. Tips: As you go to edit, start by choosing music and then editing the montage to match the pace and rhythm of the song. Video Interview: Produce a 1:00 video segment that records an interview and includes cutaway (often called “b-roll”) footage. The video should profile someone with an interesting hobby. Choose a visually appropriate space to shoot the interview, and devise open-ended questions that will allow you edit out the actual questions and just present the responses (the voice of the interviewer should NOT be heard in the video). Then, shoot your cutaway or “b-roll” footage—this footage should relate to or illustrate the topic of the interview. Edit together the interview with the cutaway footage into a polished segment. In the video, you will have the interviewee’s voice continue playing while you cut away to your other footage, so be sure you learn how to detach the audio track from the video track on your video editing software. Post the video on Vimeo or YouTube and then link to it on the assignment link in bblearn. Tips: Record more than you think you need. When shooting, start recording well before the action or interview starts and then keep shooting a few seconds after you think you are done. Keep recording more than you need. Shoot a ton. Shoot different angles and distances. Keep shooting. The cutaway footage is actually more important than the interview image. While your ratio may vary depending on your interview topic, in general you should have three to four times as much “b-roll” as “a-roll,” so about 10-15 seconds total of interview shots and about 45-50 seconds total of cutaway footage. Keep your shots short and the editing pace quick. Unless the shot has elaborate camera movements or is documenting something particularly spellbinding, no shot should be longer than 5 or 6 seconds for this assignment. 	 Video Interview (Edit): Using the feedback on the first version of the Video Interview, re-edit your video to be 30 seconds long. Post the video on Vimeo or YouTube and then link to it on the assignment link in bblearn. Process Video: Shoot and edit a 1:00 long video that documents any kind of simple process (for example, cooking a breakfast, getting ready to go to a party, etc.). Feel free to choose any topic you want (funny or silly ideas are welcome!), but make sure that your process has at least five basic steps. Consider how to efficiently depict those steps visually. Other than the title of the video, use no extra-diegetic text (no titles or intertitles)—you have to depict the process through cinematography and editing. Post the video on Vimeo or YouTube and then link to it on the assignment link in bblearn. Tips: Start wide and get closer. Establish a sense of space with wider shots before moving into closer details. Vary camera distance and angle as you document the steps. Avoid having a long sequence of close ups shot from about the same perspective as it will make the action seem jumpy. Step back at different points in the process to reveal a wider sense of the space before moving back into closer details. Cut on action. Place your edits right at the peak of different actions to make for smoother transitions. Process Video (Edit): Using the feedback on the first version of the Process Video, re-edit your video to be 30 seconds long. Post the video on Vimeo or YouTube and then link to it on the assignment link in bblearn.
